quizName: DMV Practice Test #8 30 Questions • Passing Score 24

questions.question: A proper lane position should do all of the following, except:

options.text: Help you see and be seen by others.
Help you avoid surface hazards.
Help you avoid traffic signals.
Show other drivers what you plan to do.

questions.correctAnswerText: Help you avoid traffic signals.
questions.explanation: A good lane position helps you see others and be seen. It helps you avoid wind blasts, other riders' blind spots, and surface hazards. It tells other drivers not to share your lane and gives you a way to escape if danger appears.

questions.question: In group riding, what does this hand signal mean?

options.text: Speed up.
Danger ahead.
Stop.
Merge.

questions.correctAnswerText: Stop.
questions.explanation: Hand signals help group riders communicate. When the lead rider extends their left arm straight down with palm facing back, all riders should stop.

questions.question: To see better before passing a vehicle on its left, you should:

options.text: Ride in the left portion of your lane.
Ride in the right portion of your lane.
Ride in the center portion of your lane.
Stand up on your motorcycle.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in the left portion of your lane.
questions.explanation: Ride in the left portion of your lane to see better before passing. This position helps you see ahead and makes oncoming traffic more aware of you.

questions.question: When another vehicle is passing you, you should:

options.text: Ride in the center portion of the lane.
Ride in the left portion of the lane.
Ride in the right portion of the lane.
Move between the three portions of the lane as the vehicle passes.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in the center portion of the lane.
questions.explanation: Ride in the center portion of your lane when being passed. Staying near the passing vehicle increases collision risk. Staying far from the passing vehicle may make the other driver merge back too soon.

questions.question: To stop quickly, it is best to:

options.text: Release the throttle and use the front brake.
Use the rear brake only.
Use the front brake only.
Use both brakes at the same time.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use both brakes at the same time.
questions.explanation: To stop quickly, apply both brakes at the same time.

questions.question: When approaching railroad tracks that cross your lane at an angle, it is usually safest to:

options.text: Ride straight within your lane to cross the tracks.
Turn to cross the tracks at a 90-degree angle.
Not cross the tracks on a motorcycle.
Cross the tracks by riding on the road shoulder.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride straight within your lane to cross the tracks.
questions.explanation: Ride straight through your lane when crossing angled railroad tracks. Turning to cross at a 90-degree angle is dangerous because you could drift into another lane.

questions.question: Bright-colored helmets:

options.text: Make it easier for others to see you.
Can be distracting.
Do not improve visibility.
Are not allowed.

questions.correctAnswerText: Make it easier for others to see you.
questions.explanation: A bright helmet is recommended. It protects you in a crash and helps other road users see you.

questions.question: When riding in a group, motorcyclists should:

options.text: Not worry about space cushions.
Increase their space cushions.
Reduce their space cushions by half.
Keep adequate space cushions around each rider.

questions.correctAnswerText: Keep adequate space cushions around each rider.
questions.explanation: When riding in a group, keep close ranks but still maintain an adequate space cushion around each rider.

questions.question: A motorcycle with a sidecar:

options.text: Cannot tip over.
Can tip over if turning too fast.
Can handle any turn at any speed.
Should never carry items.

questions.correctAnswerText: Can tip over if turning too fast.
questions.explanation: Even with three wheels, a sidecar can tip over if you turn too sharply or go too fast around a corner.

questions.question: The center portion of a lane often has an oily strip. This part of the lane is:

options.text: Never safe for motorcyclists.
Usually safe, unless the road is wet.
Usually safe, unless it is sunny outside.
Always safe, no matter the weather.

questions.correctAnswerText: Usually safe, unless the road is wet.
questions.explanation: Oil from cars collects in a strip in the center of traffic lanes. Unless the road is wet, this area has enough traction for safe riding. The strip is usually only two feet wide, so you can often ride to one side and still stay in the center portion of the lane.

questions.question: If your motorcycle starts to wobble, what should you do?

options.text: Brake gradually.
Speed up.
Hold the handlebars firmly and slowly close the throttle.
Shift to a lower gear.

questions.correctAnswerText: Hold the handlebars firmly and slowly close the throttle.
questions.explanation: Do not speed up during a wobble—it will make your motorcycle less stable. Instead, hold the handlebars firmly and slowly close the throttle to slow down. Move your weight forward and down. Pull off the road as soon as possible. Do not brake, as this can make the wobble worse.

questions.question: If you cannot avoid a slippery road, what should you do?

options.text: Lean into the slippery section to keep your balance.
Keep your speed steady to improve grip.
Do not worry about the road conditions.
Keep your motorcycle upright and go as slowly as needed.

questions.correctAnswerText: Keep your motorcycle upright and go as slowly as needed.
questions.explanation: The best choice is to avoid slippery roads. If you cannot avoid one, keep your motorcycle upright and go as slowly as possible.

questions.question: What type of sign is yellow with black lettering or symbols?

options.text: Warning
Service
Regulatory
Speed limit

questions.correctAnswerText: Warning
questions.explanation: Warning signs are yellow with black lettering or symbols. They alert drivers to upcoming road conditions.

questions.question: A properly-fitted motorcycle should:

options.text: Allow you to touch the ground with your feet while seated.
Have a seat level with your waist.
Have a seat 10 inches above your waist.
Have a seat 10 inches below your waist.

questions.correctAnswerText: Allow you to touch the ground with your feet while seated.
questions.explanation: A properly-fitted motorcycle lets you reach the ground with your feet while sitting on the seat. When riding, keep your feet firmly on the footrests.

questions.question: When riding over rough surfaces, you should:

options.text: Hold the handgrips loosely to allow for movement.
Hold the handgrips firmly to stay in control.
Use a lot of throttle to help get over the rough surface.
Ride without a helmet so it doesn't cover your face.

questions.correctAnswerText: Hold the handgrips firmly to stay in control.
questions.explanation: Hold the handgrips firmly when riding over rough surfaces. This keeps you in control of your motorcycle's direction.

questions.question: When should you increase your following distance?

options.text: When the pavement is dry.
When the pavement is wet.
When you can see through the vehicle ahead.
When the sun is out.

questions.correctAnswerText: When the pavement is wet.
questions.explanation: Increase your following distance when your motorcycle needs more space to stop. Do this when the pavement is slippery, when you cannot see through the vehicle ahead, or when traffic is heavy and another driver might pull in front of you.

questions.question: When passing parked cars on your right with no oncoming traffic, you should:

options.text: Stay toward the right side of your lane.
Stay toward the left side of your lane.
Look to your left frequently.
Use your rearview mirrors more often than usual.

questions.correctAnswerText: Stay toward the left side of your lane.
questions.explanation: When passing parked cars, stay away from the side where the cars are. This protects you from car doors opening or people stepping out. This gives you more space if something unexpected happens.

questions.question: To reduce your chances of a crash, you should:

options.text: Use your turn signals when you plan to change lanes.
Drive very close behind other vehicles.
Look only 15 feet ahead of your motorcycle.
Not use your headlight during the day.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use your turn signals when you plan to change lanes.
questions.explanation: To reduce crash risk, make yourself visible, use turn signals to show your plans, keep safe distances from other vehicles, look ahead at least 12 seconds, identify hazards, and be ready to react to changing conditions.

questions.question: When riding a motorcycle, you should:

options.text: Turn your head and shoulders to look through turns.
Keep your arms straight.
Keep your knees away from the gas tank.
Turn only your head and eyes to look through turns.

questions.correctAnswerText: Turn only your head and eyes to look through turns.
questions.explanation: When turning, look through the turn by turning only your head. Press your knees against the gas tank to help balance while turning. Keep your arms slightly bent when holding the handgrips.

questions.question: You will ______ hear a tire going flat.

options.text: Always
Usually
Frequently
Seldom

questions.correctAnswerText: Seldom
questions.explanation: You will seldom hear a tire going flat. You are more likely to notice tire failure by a sudden change in how your motorcycle handles.

questions.question: Where do motorcycle operators and other drivers have the most conflicts?

options.text: At intersections
On highways
On rural roads
In parking lots

questions.correctAnswerText: At intersections
questions.explanation: Intersections are where most conflicts happen between motorcyclists and other drivers. Riders should be extra careful when approaching and going through intersections.

questions.question: Most crashes happen during the day. To reduce your crash risk, you should:

options.text: Wear dark-colored clothing.
Wear bright-colored clothing.
Not ride during the day.
Look for safer routes.

questions.correctAnswerText: Wear bright-colored clothing.
questions.explanation: Wear bright colors to make yourself visible to other drivers. This reduces your crash risk, even during the day.

questions.question: When approaching an intersection, you should:

options.text: Assume other drivers see you, especially if they make eye contact.
Never assume other drivers see you.
Stay focused on moving through the intersection.
Speed up to make others notice you.

questions.correctAnswerText: Never assume other drivers see you.
questions.explanation: Never assume that other drivers see you, even if they look at you. Drivers often look directly at motorcyclists and still miss them. Always slow down when approaching an intersection.

questions.question: Before getting on your motorcycle, check everything except:

options.text: Tires
Taillight
Headlight
Paint

questions.correctAnswerText: Paint
questions.explanation: Check your tires, oil, fluids, lights, signals, clutch, throttle, mirrors, brakes, and horn before riding. Do this inspection before every ride. You do not need to check the paint.

questions.question: The front brake:

options.text: Should only be used when you need to stop quickly.
Should only be used on slippery roads.
Is not as effective as the rear brake.
Is safe to use when used correctly.

questions.correctAnswerText: Is safe to use when used correctly.
questions.explanation: Use both brakes whenever you slow down or stop. The front brake is more powerful than the rear brake. It is safe to use it if you use it correctly.

questions.question: When riding in a traffic lane, a motorcycle operator should:

options.text: Always ride in the same spot in the lane.
Change lane position based on road and traffic conditions.
Always ride in the center of the lane.
Always ride in the left part of the lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Change lane position based on road and traffic conditions.
questions.explanation: No single lane position is always best. Change your position based on the road and traffic around you.

questions.question: Moving into another lane while turning is usually caused by:

options.text: Taking the turn too fast.
Lanes that are too narrow.
Not knowing how to steer.
Lanes that are too wide.

questions.correctAnswerText: Taking the turn too fast.
questions.explanation: Going too fast into a curve or turn may cause you to cross into another lane or leave the road.

questions.question: When riding behind a car, you should:

options.text: Position yourself so the driver can see you.
Always ride in the far left part of the lane.
Not worry about where you position yourself.
Always ride in the far right part of the lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Position yourself so the driver can see you.
questions.explanation: Ride in the center of your lane when behind a car. This makes it more likely the driver will see you in their rearview mirror. Drivers check their rearview mirror more than their side mirrors.

questions.question: When riding downhill or shifting into first gear, you may need to:

options.text: Use your brakes to slow down before downshifting.
Speed up before downshifting.
Swerve to the left.
Flash your brakes to warn drivers behind you.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use your brakes to slow down before downshifting.
questions.explanation: Slow down before shifting to a lower gear. Downshifting while going too fast can cause the motorcycle to jerk and the rear wheel to skid. Use your brakes to reach a safe speed before downshifting.

questions.question: Your lane position should:

options.text: Protect your lane from other drivers.
Give you a good view of scenery.
Place you in other drivers' blind spots.
Hide your intentions from other drivers.

questions.correctAnswerText: Protect your lane from other drivers.
questions.explanation: Your lane position should keep you safe. It should keep you out of blind spots, help you see and be seen, avoid surface hazards, avoid wind from other vehicles, and give you an escape route. Position yourself so other drivers do not try to share your lane.
